title: Woman targeted by Apple support scam
description: A scammer told a Butler County woman to buy gift cards.

asr.full_text: For years, Apple owners didn't have to deal with all the scams and malware attacks that face owners of Microsoft products. You know, scammers didn't bother with Apple users, right? Well, those days are now over, as one tri-state woman learned. Stephanie Golden was shopping on her MacBook when a malware attack took over her screen. Immediately my screen went white and it said, you're at risk for spyware scam something. There was a banner underneath that said, call Apple support immediately. Panicked, she called Apple support. The agent told her he could fix her MacBook for a small fee. So I need you to go buy two gift cards. $100 gift cards, no more, no less. So she ran to the store to purchase iTunes cards. I listened because they make you feel so scared. Like your emotions kind of take over. She read the numbers to the technician, but... Those don't work. They're not coming through on our end. I don't know what's wrong. You need to go buy two more. So she bought two more, but the man said those didn't work either and that she had to buy even more. And in the end, how much did they end up with? $100 each times four. She ended up giving him $800 worth of iTunes gift cards before she realized the Apple support number she called wasn't really Apple. A few months back, we spoke with Jennifer Jansen, hit by the same scam when she thought Microsoft was on the phone. I truly believed it because my computer hasn't been working correctly. For years, the tech support scam was known as the Microsoft scam. Because it targeted people with Microsoft or Windows-based computers. But lately, those scammers have moved on to Apple devices. I'm not stupid. I'm not a gullible person. But in that moment, it was like nothing else mattered. Now she just wants to warn other Apple users. So that they don't lose hundreds of dollars like she did. Bottom line here, neither Apple or Microsoft. Or Windows will ever call you or put a pop-up on your device telling you to call them immediately,. And they will never demand immediate payment from you by credit card or iTunes gift card. So don't do it and don't waste your money. I'm John Matters, nine on your side.

textual.observation: A person presented as Apple support instructed a woman to purchase and provide multiple $100 iTunes gift-card numbers in connection with fixing her MacBook, resulting in $800 worth of gift cards being given before the called number was recognized as not really Apple.

evidence.quote: The agent told her he could fix her MacBook for a small fee. So I need you to go buy two gift cards. $100 gift cards, no more, no less.
She read the numbers to the technician, but... Those don't work. They're not coming through on our end. I don't know what's wrong. You need to go buy two more.
She ended up giving him $800 worth of iTunes gift cards before she realized the Apple support number she called wasn't really Apple.

textual.context: The source reports this as a described support scam affecting a woman; the account is presented as reporting and discussion, not as an offer to viewers.
textual.potential_relevance: The reported Apple-support identity claim is linked to urgent repeated gift-card purchases and transmission of gift-card numbers, with the source describing the destination as not really Apple.
textual.limitations: These records do not independently verify the caller's identity, the malware event, the phone number, the gift-card transactions, or the reported $800 outcome.

visual.observation: A browser-style alert visibly states that suspicious activity and a major security issue were detected, then instructs the viewer to call Apple Support immediately; the alert displays a non-Apple-looking web address ending in "windowsdesk.net" and a phone number. Later frames in the same news segment show gift-card displays and an "$800" amount.
visual.context: The visuals are presented within a news report whose lower-third headline reads "WOMAN TARGETED BY APPLE SUPPORT SCAM"; the browser alert and gift-card imagery appear as report illustrations.
visual.potential_relevance: A security-warning message links an urgent request to contact claimed Apple Support with a visible support-related web destination, while the report also presents an $800 gift-card amount, making the described contact and payment mechanism relevant for further review.
visual.limitations: These sampled frames do not establish that the woman called the number, purchased or transferred gift cards, or experienced a specific outcome. They also do not verify the web address, phone number, identity of the caller, or any transaction.

textual_context_notes.observation: The source explicitly warns that Apple, Microsoft and Windows will not call or display a pop-up directing users to call immediately, and will not demand immediate payment by credit card or iTunes gift card.
